chapters.title: The Sounds of Spanish
chapters.goal: Read any Spanish word out loud and know where the stress goes.

lessons.title: The Five Vowels
lessons.goal: Say the five Spanish vowels and read your first words out loud.

sections.title: Good news: Spanish sounds the way it looks
sections.body: In English, one letter can make many sounds (think of the "a" in cat, cake and car). Spanish is much kinder. Each vowel makes just one sound, every time. Once you know these five sounds, you can read almost any Spanish word out loud.

items.sl: oh, short and clean, like "o" in "note" without the "w" at the end

sections.title: Keep vowels short
sections.body: English speakers like to stretch vowels. We say "no" like "noh-oo." In Spanish, stop the sound clean: no. Same with "e": mesa is MEH-sah, not MAY-sah.

sections.title: How two vowels team up
sections.body: When i or u sits next to another vowel, they glide together into one beat. "ue" sounds like "weh" (bueno), "ai" sounds like "eye" (baile), and "au" sounds like "ow" (auto).

quiz.p: Which vowel sounds like the "ee" in "see"?
Which vowel sounds like the "ah" in "father"?

lessons.title: Letters That Act Differently
lessons.goal: Know the letters that do not sound like English: h, j, g, ll, y, ñ, qu and gu.

sections.title: J sounds like a breathy h
G is soft before e and i, hard before a, o, u
LL and Y sound like the "y" in "yes"
A fun difference
sections.body: In Argentina and Uruguay, ll and y sound more like "sh" or the "s" in "measure." So pollo can sound like POH-shoh. Both are correct.

sections.title: Never skip the squiggle
sections.body: Ñ is its own letter, not a fancy n. Leaving it off can change the word completely, so this app never accepts n for ñ. Año means "year."

sections.title: QU and GU: the u is silent
What about ü?
sections.body: Two dots on the u (ü) tell you to say the u after all. Without the dots, gui sounds like "gee." With the dots, güi sounds like "gwee," as in pingüino.

lessons.title: The Rolled R and Friends
lessons.goal: Tell r from rr, and say b, v, c and z the Spanish way.

items.sl: PEH-roh, with a quick tap like the "tt" in "butter"

sections.title: rr, or r at the start of a word: a roll
How to practice the roll
sections.body: Say "butter" fast, over and over: the "tt" is your tap. For the roll, rest your tongue behind your top teeth and blow air so it flutters. It takes practice. A strong tap is fine while you learn.

sections.title: B and V sound the same
C: like s before e and i, like k before a, o, u
The Spain "th"
sections.body: In most of Spain, z and the soft c sound like the "th" in "think." So cinco sounds like THEEN-koh. Latin America uses an s sound. Both are correct. Switch to Spain voices in Settings to hear it.

quiz.p: In Latin America, z sounds like...
Which two letters sound the same in Spanish?

lessons.title: Stress and Accent Marks
lessons.goal: Know which part of a word to say louder, and what an accent mark does.

sections.title: Rule 1: ends in a vowel, n or s
sections.body:
Say the second-to-last part louder.
CA-sa (house)
HA-blan (they speak)
LI-bros (books)

sections.title: Rule 2: ends in any other letter
sections.body:
Say the last part louder.
ho-TEL (hotel)
ciu-DAD (city)
ha-BLAR (to speak)

sections.title: The accent mark breaks the rules
What the mark tells you
sections.body: An accent mark (á é í ó ú) does one job: it shows the louder part when the two rules would get it wrong. It does not change the sound of the vowel. It just says "push here."

sections.title: Question words always wear one
sections.body: Words like qué (what), cómo (how) and dónde (where) always have an accent mark in a question: ¿Qué? ¿Cómo? ¿Dónde?

sections.title: Typing in this app
sections.body: If you type a word without its accent mark, the app still counts it and shows an "Almost!" note with the right spelling. Use the accent keys under the box to add them.

t.p: Type the part of "ca-sa" you say louder.
Type the part of "ho-tel" you say louder.
Type the part of "te-lé-fo-no" you say louder.
Type the part of "ciu-dad" you say louder.

quiz.p: Why does "café" have an accent mark?
quiz.a: It shows the louder part is FÉ
o: It shows the louder part is FÉ
It means the word is French
It means there is more than one

lessons.title: ¿Questions? ¡Wow!
lessons.goal: Use the upside-down marks, say the letter names and spell your name.

sections.title: Marks at both ends
sections.body:
Spanish puts an upside-down mark at the start of a question or a shout, so you know what is coming before you read it.
English: How are you? → Spanish: ¿Cómo estás?
English: Hi! → Spanish: ¡Hola!
English: How nice! → Spanish: ¡Qué bien!

sections.title: Typing them
sections.body: In this app, ¿ and ¡ are optional when you type. They are on the accent keys if you want them.

sections.title: Letter name notes
sections.body: V is "uve" in Spain and in many places, and "ve" in others. W is "doble ve" in Latin America and "uve doble" in Spain. Y was once called "i griega" (Greek i). You will hear all of them.

quiz.p: What goes at the start of a Spanish question?
Which letter name do you hear?
What is the Spanish name for the letter H?
Which letter name do you hear?
How do you say "How do you spell it?"
What is the Spanish name for the letter Q?
How do you say "My name is Ana"?
Which letter name do you hear?

lessons.title: Words You Already Know
lessons.goal: Spot words that look like English, and watch out for a few tricksters.

sections.title: Free words
sections.body: Thousands of Spanish words look almost like English ones. These are called cognates. You just need the Spanish sound.

sections.title: Three handy patterns
sections.body:
English -tion becomes -ción: nation → nación, information → información.
English -ty becomes -dad: city → ciudad, university → universidad.
English -ly becomes -mente: normally → normalmente.

sections.title: A classic mix-up
sections.body: Saying "Estoy embarazada" means "I am pregnant." Many learners have said it when they meant "I am embarrassed." Now you know!

t.p: Type the Spanish word that means "pregnant".

lessons.goal: Hear a word and pop the right bubble, then see a word and pop how it sounds. 20 questions each.

lessons.title: Optional: Spain vs Latin America
lessons.goal: Know how the two big accents differ, so nothing surprises you.

sections.title: Same language, different flavors
sections.body: Spanish in Spain and Spanish in Latin America are like British and American English. Everyone understands each other. A few sounds and words change. This app uses Latin American voices by default. You can switch to Spain voices in Settings.

sections.title: The "th" sound
sections.body: In most of Spain, z and the soft c (ce, ci) sound like the English "th" in "think." Gracias sounds like GRAH-thyahs. In Latin America it sounds like GRAH-syahs.

sections.title: "You all"
sections.body: In Latin America, ustedes means "you all" for everyone. In Spain, friends use vosotros instead. In this app, vosotros shows up grayed out and marked "Spain only," so you can recognize it.

quiz.p: In most of Spain, "cinco" starts with a sound like...
Which word means "you all" in Latin America?

chapters.title: ¡Hola! Meeting People
chapters.goal: Say hello, introduce yourself, say where you are from and tell the time.

lessons.title: Greetings and Goodbyes
lessons.goal: Say hello and goodbye, and ask how someone is.

sections.title: Which one when?
sections.body: Buenos días until about lunchtime. Buenas tardes until it gets dark. Buenas noches in the evening, and also to say good night.

quiz.p: Someone says "¿Qué tal?" Which is a good answer?
It is 9 PM. How do you greet someone?

lessons.title: Tú or Usted?
lessons.goal: Choose the friendly "you" or the polite "you."

sections.title: Two ways to say "you"
sections.body:
English has one "you." Spanish has a friendly one (tú) and a polite one (usted).
English: How are you? (to a friend) → Spanish: ¿Cómo estás?
English: How are you? (to your boss) → Spanish: ¿Cómo está usted?

sections.title: When in doubt
sections.body: Start with usted. If the other person wants you to be less formal, they will tell you, often with "Háblame de tú" (Talk to me with tú).

sections.title: What about vosotros?
sections.body: In Latin America, ustedes is "you all" for friends and strangers alike. In Spain, friends use vosotros. You will see it grayed out as "Spain only."

sections.title: Conversation
lines: Buenos días, señor Gómez. ¿Cómo está usted?
Good morning, Mr. Gómez. How are you?
Very well, thank you. And you?

sections.title: Did you notice?
sections.body: The student uses usted with the teacher, but the teacher uses tú with the student. That is very common.

quiz.p: You are talking to your best friend. Which "you"?
You are talking to a police officer. Which "you"?
How do you ask a new boss "How are you?"
How do you ask a child "What's your name?"
Which word means "you all" in Latin America?
You are talking to your grandma's neighbor for the first time. Which "you"?
How do you say "And you?" politely?

lessons.title: I Am, You Are: Ser
lessons.goal: Use the people words (I, you, he, she...) and the verb ser to say who you are and where you are from.

sections.title: Ser (to be) on the T-chart

rows.en: he is, she is, you are (polite)
rows.say: él es, ella es, usted es
ellos son, ellas son, ustedes son

sections.note: The left side is one person. The right side is more than one. The gray row is only used in Spain.

sections.title: Examples
sections.body:
English: I am a student. → Spanish: Soy estudiante.
English: I am from Mexico. → Spanish: Soy de México.
English: She is very nice. → Spanish: Ella es muy simpática.
English: We are friends. → Spanish: Somos amigos.

sections.title: You can drop yo and tú
sections.body: The verb already tells who you mean, so Spanish often leaves out yo, tú and nosotros. "Soy de Arizona" means "I am from Arizona." Also, no "a" before jobs: Soy estudiante, not "Soy un estudiante."

sections.title: Matching the person
sections.body: Most nationality words end in -o for a man and -a for a woman. Words ending in -ense stay the same for everyone. Nationalities do not start with a capital letter in Spanish.

sections.title: Conversation
lines: Hi, I'm Sofía. What's your name?
My name is Diego. Nice to meet you.
Soy de Phoenix. Soy estadounidense. ¿Y tú?
I'm from Phoenix. I'm American. And you?

quiz.p: How do you say "I am from Mexico"?

lessons.title: El, La, Un, Una
lessons.goal: Know that every noun is masculine or feminine, and pick the right "the" and "a."

sections.title: Every noun has a gender
sections.body:
In Spanish, every noun is masculine or feminine, even tables and books. The word for "the" or "a" tells you which.
English: the book → Spanish: el libro
English: the house → Spanish: la casa
English: a book → Spanish: un libro
English: a house → Spanish: una casa

sections.title: Clues from the ending
sections.body:
Ends in -o: usually masculine (el libro).
Ends in -a: usually feminine (la mesa).
Ends in -dad, -ción or -sión: feminine (la ciudad, la nación, la televisión).

sections.title: Learn the little word too
sections.body: Always learn a new noun with el or la attached: not just "mapa" but "el mapa." Then you never have to guess.

lessons.title: More Than One
lessons.goal: Make nouns plural and use los, las, unos and unas.

sections.title: Adding -s or -es
sections.body:
Ends in a vowel: add -s.
libro → libros, casa → casas
Ends in a consonant: add -es.
ciudad → ciudades, profesor → profesores
Ends in z: change z to c and add -es.
lápiz → lápices

sections.title: Examples
sections.body:
English: the books → Spanish: los libros
English: the houses → Spanish: las casas
English: some friends → Spanish: unos amigos

sections.title: Mixed groups
sections.body: For a group of boys and girls together, Spanish uses the masculine form. Los chicos can mean "the boys" or "the kids." Las chicas only means girls.

quiz.p: A group of 3 boys and 2 girls is...

lessons.title: Numbers 0 to 30
lessons.goal: Count to 30, say phone numbers and ask "how many?"

sections.title: One word, not three
sections.body: 16 to 29 are written as one word. Dieciséis is "ten and six" squeezed together. Veintidós is "twenty and two."

sections.title: Uno changes
sections.body: Before a masculine noun, uno becomes un: un libro. Before a feminine noun it becomes una: una casa.

items.sl: kwahl ehs too NOO-meh-roh deh teh-LEH-foh-noh

sections.title: Hay is handy
sections.body: Hay (said like "eye") means both "there is" and "there are." Use ¿Cuántos? for masculine things and ¿Cuántas? for feminine things.

quiz.p: How do you say "How many books are there?"

lessons.title: What Time Is It?
lessons.goal: Ask and tell the time.

sections.title: Es la or son las?
sections.body:
Use "Es la" only for one o'clock, because it is just one hour. Use "Son las" for every other hour.
English: It's 1:00. → Spanish: Es la una.
English: It's 2:00. → Spanish: Son las dos.

sections.title: Adding minutes
sections.body:
Use y (and) to add minutes, and menos (minus) to count down to the next hour.
y cuarto = quarter past
y media = half past
menos cuarto = quarter to

quiz.p: How do you say "What time is it?"

t.p: Type "It's 4:45" in Spanish, using menos cuarto.

lessons.title: Optional: Culture Corner
lessons.goal: Know how people greet each other in different Spanish-speaking places.

sections.title: A kiss, a hug or a handshake?
sections.body: In many Spanish-speaking places, friends and new acquaintances greet with a light kiss on the cheek, really more of a cheek touch with a kiss sound. Customs change by country, city, family and setting, so watch what others do and follow along.

sections.title: A rough guide
head: Place
Friends and family
Business
rows: Two cheek kisses (right cheek first). Men often shake hands.
Mexico and much of Latin America
One cheek kiss, or a hug. Men often shake hands or hug with a pat on the back.
One cheek kiss, often even between male friends.

sections.title: Saying goodbye
sections.body: The greeting often happens again when you leave. It is polite to say goodbye to each person, not just wave to the room.

quiz.p: In Spain, friends usually greet with...

t.p: Type the Spanish words for "a kiss".
Type the Spanish words for "a hug".

quiz.p: In a business meeting, most places use...

t.p: Type the Spanish words for "to shake hands".

chapters.title: At School and My Week
chapters.goal: Classes, days of the week, -ar verbs, me gusta, questions, estar and bigger numbers.

lessons.title: In the Classroom
lessons.goal: Name things in a classroom and your school subjects.

sections.title: Spain says it differently
sections.body: In Spain, a pen is often "el bolígrafo" and the board is "la pizarra." A computer is "el ordenador."

sections.title: No capitals
sections.body: Names of languages and school subjects start with a small letter in Spanish: el inglés, el español.

items.es: Hay un cuaderno y dos libros.
items.en: There is a notebook and two books.
items.sl: eye oon kwah-DEHR-noh ee dohs LEE-brohs

o: Hay un cuaderno y dos libros.

quiz.p: How do you say "the pen" (Latin America)?

lessons.title: Days of the Week
lessons.goal: Say the days, and talk about today, tomorrow and the weekend.

sections.title: Small letters, Monday first
sections.body: Days start with a small letter in Spanish. Most Spanish calendars start the week on Monday.

sections.title: On Monday or on Mondays?
sections.body:
Spanish uses el or los instead of "on."
English: on Monday (this one time) → Spanish: el lunes
English: on Mondays (every week) → Spanish: los lunes
Days ending in -s stay the same in the plural: el martes, los martes. Sábado and domingo add -s: los sábados, los domingos.

lessons.title: Action Words: -ar Verbs
lessons.goal: Use regular -ar verbs for every person.

sections.title: Chop and add
sections.body:
Verbs come with an ending: -ar, -er or -ir. To use an -ar verb, chop off -ar and add the ending for the person.
hablar → habl- → hablo (I speak)

sections.title: hablar (to speak) on the T-chart

rows.say: él habla, ella habla, usted habla
ellos hablan, ellas hablan, ustedes hablan

sections.note: The left side is one person. The right side is more than one. The gray row is only used in Spain.

sections.title: Examples
sections.body:
English: I study Spanish. → Spanish: Estudio español.
English: We work on Mondays. → Spanish: Trabajamos los lunes.
English: They dance a lot. → Spanish: Bailan mucho.
English: Do you sing? → Spanish: ¿Cantas?

sections.title: One word, many meanings
sections.body: Hablo can mean "I speak," "I do speak" or "I am speaking." Spanish does not need extra words like "do."

quiz.p: How do you say "I study Spanish"?

lessons.title: I Like It: Me Gusta
lessons.goal: Say what you like and ask what others like.

sections.title: How "gustar" works
sections.body:
Me gusta means "it pleases me." The thing you like is the subject.
English: I like coffee. → Spanish: Me gusta el café.
English: I like tacos. → Spanish: Me gustan los tacos.
English: I like to dance. → Spanish: Me gusta bailar.
One thing or an action: gusta. More than one thing: gustan.

sections.title: Keep the "the"
sections.body: Spanish keeps el, la, los or las with liked things: Me gusta la música (I like music), not "Me gusta música."

quiz.p: How do you say "Do you like music?"
How do you say "I don't like to study"?

lessons.title: Asking Questions and Saying No
lessons.goal: Ask who, what, where, when, why and how, and make a sentence negative.

sections.title: Why and because
sections.body: ¿Por qué? (two words, accent mark) asks "why?" Porque (one word, no accent) means "because."

sections.title: Saying no
sections.body:
Put no right before the verb.
English: I don't speak French. → Spanish: No hablo francés.
English: She doesn't work today. → Spanish: Ella no trabaja hoy.
To answer "no," you often say it twice: No, no trabajo hoy.

sections.title: Yes or no questions
sections.body:
Just raise your voice at the end. The words can stay the same.
English: Do you speak English? → Spanish: ¿Hablas inglés?

quiz.p: How do you say "I don't speak French"?
How do you ask "Do you speak English?"

lessons.title: Where and How: Estar
lessons.goal: Use estar to say where things are and how people are.

sections.title: A second "to be"
sections.body:
You already know ser. Estar also means "to be," but it is for where something is and how someone is right now.
English: Where is the bathroom? → Spanish: ¿Dónde está el baño?
English: I'm fine. → Spanish: Estoy bien.

sections.title: estar (to be: where and how) on the T-chart

rows.say: él está, ella está, usted está
ellos están, ellas están, ustedes están

sections.note: The left side is one person. The right side is more than one. The gray row is only used in Spain.

items.es: El libro está en la mesa.
items.en: The book is on the table.
items.sl: ehl LEE-broh ehs-TAH ehn lah MEH-sah

sections.title: Places always use estar
sections.body: Even for things that never move: Madrid está en España. You will compare ser and estar side by side in Chapter 6.

quiz.p: How do you say "Where is the bathroom?"

lessons.title: Numbers 31 and Up
lessons.goal: Count past 30, say prices and say years.

sections.title: How they fit together
sections.body:
From 31 to 99, use "y" (and): treinta y uno (31), cuarenta y cinco (45), noventa y nueve (99).
Cien is exactly 100. From 101 to 199, say ciento: ciento uno (101), ciento veinte (120).
No "y" after hundreds: doscientos diez (210).

sections.title: Years are just big numbers
sections.body: Spanish does not split years into two parts like "nineteen ninety." 1990 is "one thousand nine hundred ninety": mil novecientos noventa.

quiz.p: How do you ask "How much does it cost?"
